facts.statement: The genus Holoptychius was first described by Louis Agassiz in 1839.
facts.quote: The genus was first described by Louis Agassiz in 1839.

facts.statement: Holoptychius was a streamlined predator that fed on other bony fish, growing from about 50 cm to a maximum of 2.5 meters in length.
facts.quote: Holoptychius was a streamlined predator about 50 cm long (though largest specimen could grow up to 2.5 m), which fed on other bony fish.

facts.statement: Holoptychius had rounded scales and a body form suggesting it could swim quickly to catch prey.
facts.quote: Its rounded scales and body form indicate that it could have swum quickly through the water to catch prey.

facts.statement: Like other rhipidistians, Holoptychius possessed fang-like teeth on its palate and smaller teeth on its jaws.
facts.quote: Similar to other rhipidistians, it had fang-like teeth on its palate in addition to smaller teeth on the jaws.

facts.statement: Holoptychius had an asymmetrical tail with a caudal fin located on the lower end.
facts.quote: Its asymmetrical tail sported a caudal fin on its lower end.

facts.statement: To counteract the downward push of its lower caudal fin, Holoptychius had its pectoral fins positioned high on its body.
facts.quote: To compensate for the downward push caused by this fin placement, the pectoral fins of Holoptychius were placed high on the body.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Holoptychius was likely an ambush predator with a lifestyle similar to the modern arapaima.
facts.quote: It was likely an ambush predator with a similar lifestyle to the modern arapaima.

facts.statement: Fossils of Holoptychius have been found worldwide, including North America, South America, and much of Europe.
facts.quote: It is known from fossils worldwide, from North America, South America, and much of Europe.

facts.statement: Isotopic analysis of remains from Greenland suggests Holoptychius was likely a euryhaline organism capable of living in varying salinities.
facts.quote: Isotopic analysis of Holoptychius remains from Greenland reveals that it was likely a euryhaline organism.

facts.statement: H. bergmanni is a valid species of Holoptychius known from Frasnian fossils in Ellesmere Island, Arctic Canada.
facts.quote: Only the following valid species are known by diagnostic remains: H. bergmanni Downs, Daeschler, Jenkins & Shubin, 2013 - Frasnian of Ellesmere Island, Arctic Canada (Fram Formation)

facts.statement: H. flemingi is a valid species found in Famennian deposits in Scotland and Belgium.
facts.quote: H. flemingi Agassiz, 1844 - Famennian of Scotland (Glenvale Sandstone) & Belgium (Evieux Formation)

facts.statement: H. jarviki is a valid species known from Frasnian fossils in Quebec, Canada.
facts.quote: H. jarviki Cloutier & Schultze, 1996 - Frasnian of Quebec, Canada (Escuminac Formation)

facts.statement: H. nobilissimus is the type species of Holoptychius, found in Late Frasnian to early Famennian rocks in Scotland, England, Latvia, Norway, and Russia.
facts.quote: H. nobilissimus Agassiz, 1839 (type species) - Late Frasnian to early Famennian of Scotland & England (Old Red Sandstone), potentially Latvia (Ketleri Formation), Norway & Oryol Oblast in Russia (Turgenevo Formation)

facts.statement: H. jarviki was previously often called H. quebecensis before being described as a distinct species in 1996 after its material was separated from Quebecius quebecensis.
facts.quote: In past sources, H. jarviki was frequently referred to as H. quebecensis, due to its material being conflated with that of Quebecius quebecensis, necessitating its description as a distinct species in 1996.

facts.statement: The genus Glytolepis was formerly treated as a subgenus of Holoptychius.
facts.quote: The genus Glytolepis was also previously treated as a subgenus of Holoptychius.

facts.statement: Holoptychius fossils have been discovered in Belgium, Colombia, Norway, Canada, Russia, Greenland, and the United States.
facts.quote: Fossils of Holoptychius have been found in the Devonian of Belgium, Colombia (Boyacá), Norway, Canada (Quebec & New Brunswick), the Russian Federation (Oryol), Greenland, and the United States (New York & Pennsylvania).
